title: SM throttle recovery and decode throughput across cloud SKUs
content:
Summary:

This working note captures a focused set of experiments exploring SM (streaming multiprocessor) clock throttling behavior and post-throttle recovery effects on decode throughput for long-context autoregressive workloads. We ran identical model-decode workloads across common cloud GPU SKUs representing A100, H100 and L40S lines and swept driver/CUDA stacks and power governor settings. The goal was to understand: (1) when and why SM clocks drop under steady decode, (2) the transient throughput and tail-latency impact during and after throttle events, and (3) mitigations (config knobs or runtime patterns) that reduce unit-cost/regression risk in production serving.

Why this matters (background):
- Our serving runtime aggressively packs prefills + streaming decode. Long-context KV warmups + sustained decoding can push power/thermal boundaries on some cloud SKUs.
- SM clock drops (thermal or power budget induced) lead to step-function throughput regressions and elevated p99 latencies that survive the immediate event due to kernel cache warmp-up and scheduler rebalancing.
- Customers opt for different SKUs/regions: we need repeatable guidance and runtime fallback heuristics.

Hypotheses:
- H1: Older driver + CUDA stacks (e.g., CUDA 11.8 + driver 525.x) show higher incidence of SM clock throttling on A100 under >90% sustained tensor utilization compared to later drivers.
- H2: H100 exhibits better SM clock stability for steady decode workloads, but when it does throttle, recovery is slower due to deeper DVFS steps.
- H3: L40S (data center inference card) will show fewer throttle events at default power limits but will have larger throughput delta between nominal and throttled clocks.

Testbed and controlled variables:
- GPUs and SKUs tested (representative):
  - AWS p4d (8x A100 40GB) single-GPU experiments using a pinned instance: a100-40gb
  - GCP a3/h2 style H100 instances (single H100) labeled h100-80gb-equivalent
  - Azure L40s instances single-L40s
- Drivers/CUDA: tested combinations
  - CUDA 11.8 + NVIDIA driver 525.85
  - CUDA 12.1 + NVIDIA driver 535.113
  - CUDA 12.2 + NVIDIA driver 545.30 (where available)
- Power governors and limits: default auto, enforced power cap (e.g., 250W for A100 reference), and tuned higher cap where permitted.
- Workload: GPT-like decoder microbenchmark:
  - Prefill tokens: 2k (randomized content but deterministic length)
  - Streaming decode: generate 512 tokens with temperature 0.0 (deterministic), batch sizes of 1, 4, 8 to test small and medium packing behaviors
  - KV cache ephemeral size matched to prompt length to ensure memory pressure scenarios
- Telemetry: NVML sampled at 100ms, perf events for SM utilization, per-kernel timestamps from our runtime traces, host-level power and fan RPMs. p50/p90/p99 decode per-token latency aggregated across 1h runs.

Experiment matrix (brief):
- For each SKU x driver/CUDA combo x power cap x batch-size run a 1h sustained decode workload loop that repeats prefill+decode.
- Reproduce each cell 3 times to check variance.

Key observations (condensed):
1) A100 behavior:
- With CUDA 11.8 + driver 525: observed repeated SM clock drops after 9–12 minutes of sustained runs for batch sizes >=4. SM clock step-downs were ~150–200 MHz. Aggregate decode throughput dropped by 12–20% during throttled periods. p99 token latency increased by 1.6–2.3x relative to pre-throttle steady state.
- Upgrading to CUDA 12.1 + driver 535 reduced frequency of events by ~60% and reduced magnitude of clock step downs (~80–120 MHz), with throughput impact reduced to 5–10%.
- Applying a conservative power cap (slightly lower than factory default) prevented many throttle events but caused an immediate baseline throughput reduction (3–6%) due to lower sustained clocks; net effect balanced out vs uncontrolled throttle.

2) H100 behavior:
- H100 under CUDA 12.1/535 showed fewer throttle triggers than A100 for identical workload intensity. When H100 did experience throttling, clock steps were fewer but deeper (e.g., single-step drop of 300 MHz).
- Recovery time from a throttle event (NVML reports clocks stabilizing) was longer on H100: measured wall-clock recovery of 45–90s where throughput only slowly climbed back to baseline over several hundred decode calls. This produced noticeable streaks of elevated per-token latency for user requests.

3) L40S behavior:
- L40S kept clocks more stable under the same synthetic load at default factory power. When we raised workload intensity (simulated multiple tenant streams), L40S showed abrupt throughput cliffs: the delta between nominal and throttled throughput was larger (20–30%) compared to A100/H100.

4) Driver/CUDA interplay:
- Newer driver stacks improved both incidence and magnitude but did not eliminate events on all SKUs. There appears to be a combination of firmware/driver hysteresis and kernel launch patterns that affects whether the GPU falls back to a lower clock bin.

5) Runtime-level interactions and kernel warmup:
- After throttle, the serving runtime experienced transient kernel launcher backpressure and suboptimal kernel scheduling (more small kernels instead of coalesced ones), which increased overhead for several dozen decode steps even after SM clocks returned to nominal.
- Continuous batching helped smooth small oscillations but amplified the tail effect when a throttle event occurred because larger batched kernels were more sensitive to clock steps.

Representative numbers (single-GPU, batch=4, CUDA11.8/driver525):
- A100: baseline decode throughput 125 tokens/s -> throttled 102 tokens/s (−18%), p99 latency pre 210ms -> post 480ms
- H100: baseline 210 tokens/s -> throttled 170 tokens/s (−19%), p99 latency pre 120ms -> post 300ms (longer recovery window)
- L40S: baseline 160 tokens/s -> throttled 120 tokens/s (−25%), p99 latency pre 150ms -> post 420ms
(These numbers are illustrative averages across runs; variance noted in full logs.)

Short runtime experiment log snippets (examples):
- nvml sample snippet: time=00:10:42, sm_clock=1140 MHz, util=98%, power=320W, event=sm_throttle_true
- kernel-level trace: spike in kernel launch rate at t=00:10:41, followed by increased kernel duration and queue length at t=00:10:43

Interpretation and root causes (working hypotheses):
- Thermal vs Power domain: Some SKUs are hitting power budget constraints (host/power delivery, platform-level caps) while others show thermal governor transitions. Distinguishing the two requires platform telemetry (host VRM readings) which we only partially have for cloud instances.
- Driver hysteresis: older drivers tend to be less aggressive about smoothing frequency but may oscillate; newer drivers improve stability but still step down under extreme sustained utilization.
- Kernel sensitivity: larger batched kernels have heavier sensitivity to clock shifts; smaller, steady kernels mask gradual clock variations better.

Immediate recommendations for serving runtime (practical):
1) Telemetry-first fallback: add an automatic short-circuit when per-gpu sm_clock delta > X and sustained for >Y seconds — trigger lighter decode path (e.g., reduce batch packing for a short cooldown) and emit an alert.
2) Warm-up smoothing: perform a staged ramp to full batch size over 30–60s for long-prefill requests to avoid sudden jumps that trigger platform governors.
3) Power-aware routing: prefer SKUs known for better stability for long sustained workloads (H100 with newer driver or L40S with controlled tenant consolidation), or use dedicated capacity where power/thermal settings can be tuned.
4) Driver baseline: require CUDA>=12.1 + driver 535+ as baseline for long-context decode workloads in our hosted API benches; flag older stacks as higher-risk.
5) Kernel packing heuristics: fall back to smaller per-call batch sizes when NVML shows approaching thermal/power thresholds; automatically re-enable packing after recovery window.

Open action items / next experiments:
- Add host-level power telemetry where possible (contact cloud partners) to separate thermal vs power-capping.
- Re-run the matrix under a continuous mixed-tenant workload (90% short requests, 10% long ones) to see interaction effects.
- Prototype a runtime throttle-detection circuit (simple NVML-based) and test its false positive rate for live traffic.
- Share summarized benchmark with Solutions Eng for SKU selection guidance.

Notes to self / caveats:
- Cloud instance OEM firmware and host power delivery differences likely explain inter-region variance. Do not overgeneralize single-region results.
- Numbers point to patterns but are sensitive to ambient data center conditions and fan curves; treat absolute dq numbers as indicative rather than prescriptive.

Appendix: experiment commands used (examples)
- nvprof / nvml sampling: python scripts/nvml-sampler.py --interval 0.1 --out=run1.csv
- launch workload: ./serve_bench --model gpt-small --prefill 2000 --decode 512 --batch 4 --repeat 3600 --cuda 12.1
